why: Same idea as cad-0002 (aspirin is the first drug in acute MI)

set.explanation: Nitrates are contraindicated within 48 hours of tadalafil (24 hours for sildenafil), because PDE-5 inhibitors potentiate nitric-oxide-mediated vasodilatation and the combination can cause profound, even fatal, hypotension. Aspirin, a P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulation and a beta-blocker (he is normotensive with no heart failure) are all appropriate for this NSTEMI; pain can be treated with IV opioids instead.

why: Same idea as cad-0036 (the 12-lead ECG is the first and decisive test in suspected STEMI)

set.explanation: Cardiac troponin I or T, ideally with a high-sensitivity assay, is the preferred biomarker for MI because it is highly sensitive and specific for myocardial injury. The universal definition of MI requires a rise and/or fall with at least one value above the 99th centile, together with ischaemic symptoms or ECG or imaging evidence. CK-MB and LDH are less specific and are rarely needed now, and ESR is non-specific.

set.stem: During coronary angiography a catheter-tip thrombus embolises and completely occludes the left anterior descending artery. If it were not removed, when would CK-MB first be expected to rise in a standard serum assay?
set.explanation: CK-MB starts to rise 4–8 hours after the onset of infarction, peaks at about 24 hours and returns to normal within 48–72 hours, which makes it useful for detecting reinfarction. Troponin rises over a similar time (earlier with high-sensitivity assays) but stays raised for 7–14 days. Myoglobin rises earliest (1–2 hours) but is not specific.

The largest delay in STEMI care is usually the patient's own delay in recognising symptoms and calling for help, often an hour or more, and it is longest in older people, women and people with diabetes. System delays (ambulance response, door-to-balloon time) are now short in organised networks, which is why public education about symptoms is so important.

Failure of the ST elevation to resolve by at least 50% within 60–90 minutes of fibrinolysis, with ongoing pain, indicates failed reperfusion; the patient should have immediate rescue PCI. Repeat fibrinolysis (including streptokinase) is ineffective and increases bleeding, emergency CABG is only for unsuitable anatomy or mechanical complications, and waiting increases infarct size.

set.stem: A 65-year-old woman with hypertension has exertional breathlessness and chest pressure after 2–3 blocks. Angiography shows high-grade focal stenoses in the proximal LAD, circumflex and right coronary arteries. When counselling her about PCI versus CABG, which statement is true?
set.explanation: The choice between PCI and CABG in multivessel disease depends on anatomical complexity (SYNTAX score), diabetes, LV function, comorbidity and the likelihood of complete revascularisation; a heart-team discussion is recommended. At 1 year mortality is similar; CABG carries a slightly higher early stroke risk, while PCI needs more repeat revascularisation.

set.stem: A man with exertional chest pressure has infero-apico-posterior ischaemia on a perfusion scan. Angiography shows a left-dominant system with a chronic total occlusion (CTO) of the circumflex artery, filled by collaterals from the LAD; the operator cannot cross it with an antegrade wire. Which statement about treating the CTO is true?
set.explanation: When antegrade wiring fails, experienced operators can approach a CTO retrogradely through septal or epicardial collaterals, and this has greatly improved success rates. Successful CTO revascularisation relieves angina and can improve regional LV function, and surgical grafting of the distal vessel is usually feasible. Randomised evidence that CTO-PCI reduces mortality is lacking.

set.stem: A 67-year-old man had CABG 12 years ago (LIMA to LAD and three saphenous vein grafts). He now has a month of crescendo angina, and angiography shows a significant stenosis in the body of the vein graft to the first obtuse marginal branch. Which statement is true?
set.explanation: Degenerated vein grafts contain friable atheroma, and PCI to them carries a high risk of distal embolisation and no-reflow, so embolic protection devices should be used where feasible. Late vein-graft failure is due to accelerated atherosclerosis rather than embolism from the anastomosis. LIMA grafts have far better long-term patency than vein grafts (over 90% versus about 50–60% at 10 years).

set.stem: A 75-year-old man has diagnostic coronary angiography via the femoral artery. A week later he has abdominal pain, nausea and reduced urine output, a temperature of 38.3°C and livedo reticularis on both legs. Creatinine is 2.7 mg/dL (previously 1.1), eosinophils 21% and ESR 92 mm/h. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Atheroembolic (cholesterol crystal) disease follows catheter manipulation of an atheromatous aorta, usually days to weeks later, with livedo reticularis, blue toes, abdominal pain, acute kidney injury, eosinophilia, a raised ESR and low complement. Contrast nephropathy starts within 48–72 hours without eosinophilia or a rash, and interstitial nephritis follows a drug exposure. Treatment is supportive, with statins and avoiding anticoagulation.

set.stem: A 75-year-old smoker with diabetes and hypertension has burning calf pain after walking two blocks, relieved by rest, and nocturnal calf aching relieved by sitting up. Which statement is most likely true?
options: His pulse-volume recording will be sharp and spiked
The most likely cause is fibromuscular dysplasia of the femoral arteries
The next investigation should be MR angiography
His ankle–brachial pressure index is likely to be below 0.9
set.explanation: Claudication with rest pain relieved by dependency in a smoker with diabetes is atherosclerotic PAD, and the first test is the ankle–brachial pressure index: below 0.9 confirms PAD, and below 0.4 suggests critical ischaemia (it may be falsely high in diabetes because of calcified vessels). Pulse-volume waveforms become flattened, not spiked. MR or CT angiography is only needed when revascularisation is planned.

why: Truncated option restored ('less than 0.9'); stem condensed

set.stem: A 75-year-old smoker with diabetes and hypertension has symptomatic peripheral arterial disease with an ankle–brachial index of 0.82 on both sides. Which statement about his prognosis and treatment is true?
set.explanation: Supervised exercise, walking to near-maximal claudication pain before resting and repeating for 30–60 minutes several times a week, improves walking distance and is first-line therapy (NICE CG147). His main risk over 5 years is death from MI or stroke; only about 1–2% a year progress to critical limb ischaemia. Antiplatelet therapy (clopidogrel) is preferred to warfarin, cardioselective beta-blockers are safe, and vasodilators have no proven benefit.

why: Source key D (progression to critical limb ischaemia) is wrong; cardiovascular events dominate prognosis. Key changed to supervised exercise; stem made self-contained

set.explanation: A young smoker with distal upper-limb ischaemia, digital changes and smooth, tapering segmental occlusions of small distal arteries has thromboangiitis obliterans. Complete abstinence from tobacco, including nicotine replacement, is the only intervention that halts progression and prevents amputation. Anticoagulants, steroids and cilostazol are ineffective, and revascularisation is rarely possible because of the distal disease.

Varicose veins are more common in women, whereas chronic venous insufficiency with oedema is slightly more common in men in population studies. Chronic venous disease becomes common with age, but most patients never develop ulcers: active or healed venous ulcers affect only about 1–2% of adults.

The great (long) saphenous vein runs from the medial end of the dorsal venous arch, anterior to the medial malleolus, up the medial leg and thigh to join the femoral vein at the saphenofemoral junction, making it the longest vein in the body. Its length and superficial position make it the conduit most often used for coronary bypass grafts, and it is the vein most often affected by varicosities.

An ulcer over the medial malleolus with hyperpigmentation (haemosiderin), woody induration (lipodermatosclerosis) and oedema after a DVT is a venous ulcer from chronic venous insufficiency. It is treated with compression bandaging, once the ABPI confirms adequate arterial supply, together with leg elevation and referral for superficial venous surgery. Arterial ulcers are painful, punched-out and on the toes or pressure areas, and diabetic ulcers occur on pressure points of a neuropathic foot.

set.stem: A 48-year-old woman has a routine health check: total cholesterol 5.8 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.7 mmol/L, BMI 29 kg/m2, non-smoker, 10 units of alcohol a week, no personal or family history, and a QRISK3 score of 12%. Which step in her initial management is LEAST needed?
set.explanation: NICE advises that everyone at raised cardiovascular risk first receives lifestyle advice: a cardioprotective diet with unsaturated fats, reduced refined carbohydrate, regular aerobic exercise and weight loss. For a QRISK3 of 10% or more, atorvastatin 20 mg is then offered as part of a shared decision, but it is not the first step in initial management, and many choose to try lifestyle change before starting a statin.

Invasive coronary angiography is the definitive (reference-standard) test for coronary anatomy and allows revascularisation in the same procedure. In practice NICE recommends CT coronary angiography first for suspected stable angina, and functional tests (stress echo, perfusion scintigraphy or MRI) when CT is non-diagnostic. A resting echo or an ECG during pain cannot define the coronary anatomy.

Fibrinolysis is indicated for STEMI within 12 hours of symptom onset when primary PCI cannot be performed within 120 minutes, and it is most effective in the first 3 hours. Beyond 12 hours it is not routinely given; ongoing ischaemia beyond this window is treated with PCI instead.

Blue, painful toes with livedo reticularis but palpable major pulses in an arteriopath after anticoagulation or arterial instrumentation is cholesterol (atheroembolic) embolisation; the crystals block small arterioles. It may also cause acute kidney injury, eosinophilia and gut ischaemia. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia causes large-vessel thrombosis and a falling platelet count, and haemorrhage does not produce a lace-like pattern.

why: Same idea as cad-0069 (ischaemic heart disease is the commonest cause of heart failure)

set.explanation: Hyperlipidaemia, smoking, hypertension and raised homocysteine are associated with ischaemic heart disease. Dietary folic acid lowers homocysteine and is not a risk factor, although folate supplements have not reduced coronary events in trials.

Typical angina with ischaemic ST depression on exercise but normal epicardial coronary arteries on angiography is cardiac syndrome X, or microvascular angina, caused by coronary microvascular dysfunction; it is more common in women. Prinzmetal angina causes transient ST elevation at rest from epicardial spasm. Stable and unstable angina imply obstructive coronary disease.

Treatment-dose enoxaparin for ACS is 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours, reduced to once daily if the creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min. 40 mg once daily is the thromboprophylaxis dose, and 1.5 mg/kg once daily is used for venous thromboembolism. Fondaparinux 2.5 mg daily is preferred by NICE and ESC when early angiography is not planned, because it causes less bleeding.

An attack of stable angina is treated with sublingual GTN; if the pain persists 5 minutes after a second dose, an ambulance should be called and ACS considered. Beta-blockers or rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers are the first-line drugs to prevent attacks, nicorandil is an add-on, and aspirin is for secondary prevention rather than pain relief.

The inferior wall is seen by leads II, III and aVF, and is usually supplied by the right coronary artery. Septal changes appear in V1–V2 (V1–V3 anteroseptal), anterior in V3–V4, and lateral in I, aVL, V5 and V6. Old Q waves in a territory indicate a previous transmural infarct.

The posterior wall has no direct standard lead, so infarction appears as a mirror image in V1–V2: tall, broad R waves (the reciprocal of Q waves), horizontal ST depression and upright tall T waves. Posterior leads V7–V9 show ST elevation and confirm it, and it is treated as a STEMI equivalent requiring reperfusion. Posterior infarction usually follows circumflex or RCA occlusion.

why: Same idea as cad-0077 (troponin is the preferred biomarker of MI)

set.explanation: Reperfusion (primary PCI, or fibrinolysis if PCI is not available in time) is indicated for ischaemic symptoms with ST elevation in two contiguous leads, or presumed new LBBB, or a true posterior MI. Widespread ST depression, isolated Q waves, RBBB or QT prolongation are not indications for fibrinolysis, which can harm patients without an occluded artery.

why: Same idea as cad-0002 (aspirin is the first drug in suspected MI)

set.stem: A 43-year-old man has an acute MI treated with immediate angioplasty. All of the following are LATE complications of myocardial infarction (weeks to months) EXCEPT:
set.explanation: Ventricular septal rupture, like free-wall and papillary muscle rupture, is an early mechanical complication, typically 2–7 days after infarction when the necrotic myocardium is weakest. Dressler syndrome (autoimmune pericarditis), LV aneurysm, mural thrombus with embolism and chronic heart failure develop weeks to months later.

why: Original options had two defensible answers (early pericarditis and VSD rupture are both early complications); rewritten with an unambiguous key

set.explanation: The left circumflex artery supplies the lateral wall (and, in left-dominant systems, the inferior and posterior walls), so isolated occlusion typically causes ST elevation in the lateral leads I, aVL, V5 and V6, often with posterior changes (ST depression in V1–V3). Circumflex infarcts are the most likely to be electrically 'silent' on the standard ECG. RCA occlusion gives inferior ST elevation and LAD occlusion anterior changes.

options: Immediate angiography with stenting within 2 hours
Discharge with an outpatient exercise test
set.explanation: New rest pain with inferior ST depression and T-wave inversion but normal troponin is unstable angina. Anticoagulation with LMWH or fondaparinux is added to aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor, and angiography is planned according to risk. Fibrinolysis is harmful without ST elevation, nicardipine has no outcome benefit, immediate (<2 h) angiography is only for very high-risk features, and discharge is unsafe.

why: Original option 'oral clopidogrel' was also correct (dual antiplatelet therapy is standard); options rewritten so only one answer is right

set.explanation: Twenty minutes into an occlusive infarct, the earliest diagnostic change is ST elevation (after hyperacute T waves). Troponin may not yet have risen, pathological Q waves take hours to develop, and ST depression or T-wave inversion indicate ischaemia or NSTE-ACS rather than acute transmural infarction.

In true aspirin hypersensitivity, clopidogrel (or another P2Y12 inhibitor) is used as the antiplatelet agent in ACS, together with anticoagulation and reperfusion as indicated; aspirin desensitisation may be considered later. Morphine only relieves pain, warfarin is not an ACS treatment, and dipyridamole has no role in acute MI.

why: Heparin, originally an option, is also part of ACS management; replaced with dipyridamole so only one answer is right

set.explanation: Recurrent rest pain in the early morning, without exertional symptoms, with transient ST elevation, no troponin rise and normal coronary arteries is vasospastic (variant, Prinzmetal) angina, caused by coronary artery spasm. It is associated with smoking, cocaine and triptans and is treated with calcium-channel blockers and nitrates; beta-blockers can worsen spasm.

ST elevation in II, III and aVF is an inferior STEMI, which in about 80% of people is caused by right coronary artery occlusion (the circumflex in left-dominant systems). Look also for right ventricular infarction (ST elevation in V4R, hypotension, clear lungs), which is managed with fluids and by avoiding nitrates.
